1.q: בְּ⁠עֶשְׂרִ֣ים וְ⁠חָמֵ֣שׁ שָׁנָ֣ה לְ֠⁠גָלוּתֵ⁠נוּ בְּ⁠רֹ֨אשׁ הַ⁠שָּׁנָ֜ה בֶּ⁠עָשׂ֣וֹר לַ⁠חֹ֗דֶשׁ בְּ⁠אַרְבַּ֤ע עֶשְׂרֵה֙ שָׁנָ֔ה אַחַ֕ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר הֻכְּתָ֖ה הָ⁠עִ֑יר בְּ⁠עֶ֣צֶם הַ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֗ה
1.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about what happened to Ezekiel before the information about when it happened. Alternate translation: [The hand of Yahweh was upon me and he brought me there on the tenth of the month at the head of the year, in year 25 of our exile, in year 14 after the city was struck, on that very day]
If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **tenth**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [on day ten of the month]

Ezekiel is using **in the head of the year** as a common expression of the culture to mean “at the beginning of the year.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at the beginning of the year]

Ezekiel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [on the tenth day of the month]

Ezekiel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [on the tenth day of the month]

The expression **was struck** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, it is clear from the context that the Babylonians did it. Alternate translation: [after the Babylonians struck the city]

The implication is that **the city** is Jerusalem and that **was struck** means that it was captured and destroyed. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [after the city of Jerusalem was captured and destroyed]

Here, **hand** represents “power.” Ezekiel means that it was the power of Yahweh that was controlling him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s power controlled me]

The word **there** refers to the city of Jerusalem, which Ezekiel has just mentioned. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. This also is referenced in verse 3. Alternate translation: [and he brought me to that city]

2.note: See how you translated this phrase, “visions of God” in [1:1](ta:01). Alternate translation: [In visions that God gave me]

Ezekiel is using **he made me rest to a very high mountain** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he set me down on a very high mountain.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he set me down on a very high mountain]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a city** has many buildings arranged together, so what Ezekiel saw on the mountain had many buildings arranged together. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [were many buildings that were arranged together]

3.note: Ezekiel is using the term **behold** to express his surprise at what he saw. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and there was a man!]

Ezekiel is introducing **a man** as a new participant in the story. This is the man who guides Ezekiel through the rest of the vision. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation.

The point of this comparison is that just as polished **bronze** shines brightly, so the man’s **appearance** shone brightly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [He appeared to shine as brightly as polished bronze]

A **cord of linen** was a long rope made from linen that people used to measure long distances, and **the reed of the measurement** was a long stick used to measure shorter distances. If your readers would not be familiar with these things, you could use the names of similar things that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [and a long measuring rope was in his hand and a measuring stick]

4.note: Yahweh is using **son of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “human being.” See the Introduction to Ezekiel for more information on this form of address. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST. See how you translated “son of man” in [2:1](ta:02).

It might seem that the expression **see with your eyes, and with your ears hear** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [see and hear]

The man is using **set your heart to** as a common expression of the culture to mean to think carefully about or determine to understand something. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and determine to understand all]
Here, **in order to** marks **make you see** as the goal or purpose of **you were brought here**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.
Here, **in order to** marks **make you see** as the goal or purpose of **you were brought here**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

The expression **were brought** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, it is clear from the context that Yahweh did it. Alternate translation: [Yahweh brought you here]

The man is speaking of all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel, as if they were all one **house**, or household, living together. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to all the people descended from Israel]

5.note: The implication is that **the house** refers to the temple. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a wall on the outside of the temple area that went]

Ezekiel is repeating the word **around** in order to intensify the idea that it conveys. He means that the wall went completely around the temple. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. This also occurs throughout the description of this vision. Alternate translation: [completely around]

5.q: קְנֵ֣ה הַ⁠מִּדָּ֗ה שֵׁשׁ אַמּ֤וֹת בָּֽ⁠אַמָּה֙ וָ⁠טֹ֔פַח
5.note: These **cubits** were a unit of measurement corresponding to the distance between an average person’s elbow and middle fingertip, or about 46 centimeters or 18 inches. A **handbreadth** was a unit of measurement corresponding to the width of an average person’s hand, or about 8 centimeters or 3 inches. Ezekiel means that each cubit of this measuring reed was a regular cubit plus a handbreadth, or about 54 centimeters or 21 inches, so that the whole reed was about 3.2 meters or 10.5 feet long. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express these lengths in modern measurements, either in the text or a footnote. Alternate translation: [the measuring reed was about 3.2 meters or 10.5 feet long]

The implication is that **the structure** is the **wall** that Ezekiel just mentioned, so **the width** is the thickness of that wall. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the thickness of the wall]

5.q: אֶת־רֹ֤חַב הַ⁠בִּנְיָן֙ קָנֶ֣ה אֶחָ֔ד וְ⁠קוֹמָ֖ה קָנֶ֥ה אֶחָֽד
5.note: Ezekiel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the width of the structure was one reed and the height was one reed]

6.note: Here, Ezekiel uses **gate**, to mean the whole structure around the gate, or a gatehouse. Since this has “steps” leading to it and windows or niches in it, it is more than just the gate itself. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a structure around the gate]

By **whose face was the way to the east**, Ezekiel means that it was facing east. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a gate that faced east]

6.q: קָנֶ֤ה אֶחָד֙ רֹ֔חַב וְ⁠אֵת֙ סַ֣ף אֶחָ֔ד קָנֶ֥ה אֶחָ֖ד רֹֽחַב
6.note: Here, the phrase **and one sill, one reed in width** could be: (1) a restatement of the measurement. In this case, you may not need to express this phrase explicitly. Alternate translation: [one reed wide] (2) a measurement for the sill for the doors that opened into the courtyard. In this case, the first sill is the sill for the doors that opened outside the wall. Alternate translation: [one reed wide, and the inner sill, one reed wide] (3) a measurement for other side of the sill. In this case, the first measurement is for one side of the sill and the other measurement for the other side. Alternate translation: [one reed on both sides]

7.note: An **alcove** was a small recess in the side wall of the gateway where guards stood. If your readers would not be familiar with what an alcove is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [And each alcove, which was a small room for guards,]

The implication is that **from the house** means that this sill was at the end of the gateway that was closest to the temple building, next to **the porch of the gate**. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the gate at the end nearest the temple building, beside the porch of the gate]

8.note: Some ancient manuscripts read **from the house, one reed**. The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read only “from the house.” The UST follows that reading. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the UST.

A **porch** was a kind of covered entrance outside a door or gate. Here it was at the inner end of the gateway and opened into the outer court. If your readers would not be familiar with what a porch is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. This also occurs in verse 9. Alternate translation: [the covered entrance of the gateway]

9.note: Some ancient manuscripts read **And he measured the porch of the gate, eight cubits**. The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read only “eight cubits,” rather than duplicating the words “And he measured the porch of the gate” from verse 8. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the UST.

A **jamb** was a kind of thick wall on each side of an opening, a doorway, or a gateway. If your readers would not be familiar with what a jamb is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. This also occurs throughout the rest of the chapter. Alternate translation: [and its side wall was two cubits thick]

The phrase **its jamb** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. There is, however, a correction to make it plural in the margin of the text that Hebrew scribes have recommended. You may want to follow this correction in your translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Here and throughout the chapter, the UST follows the correction in the margin and makes it plural. See the chapter introduction for more information. Alternate translation: [and its jambs]
See how you translated these similar phrases, “the porch of the gate from the house,” in verse 7.

10.note: The expression “from here and from there” means “on each side,” so the phrase **three from here and three from there** means that there were three alcoves on each side. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [were three on one side and three on the other side]

The implication is that all three of the **alcoves** on each side were the same size. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [one measurement for all three alcoves on each side]
By **the way of the east**, Ezekiel means on the east side. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation as in the UST if that would be helpful to your readers.

The implication is that the **jambs** on each side were the same size. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the jambs on one side were the same size as the jambs on the other side]

11.note: This could mean: (1) how wide the passage through the gate was. In this case, the opening is narrower than this passage, probably because the doors take up space at the sides of the opening, Alternate translation: [The width of the passage through the gate] or (2) how long or deep the passage through the opening was. However, the total numbers do not add up well with this interpretation. Alternate translation: [The depth of the opening of the gate]

12.note: A **border** was a kind of low wall or curb in front of the **alcoves**. If your readers would not be familiar with what a border is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [And a low wall called a border]

This could mean: (1) that each **border** on both sides of the hallway was **one cubit** wide. It is not clear if this refers to the thickness of the wall or its length, Alternate translation: [one cubit wide, and one cubit wide each border on the other side] or (2) that each **border** on both sides of the hallway was **one cubit** high, Alternate translation: [one cubit high, and one cubit high each border on the other side] or (3) that each **border** was **one cubit** wide and **one cubit** deep. Alternate translation: [one cubit wide and one cubit deep]

12.q: שֵׁשׁ אַמּ֣וֹת מִ⁠פּ֔וֹ וְ⁠שֵׁ֥שׁ אַמּ֖וֹת מִ⁠פּֽוֹ
12.note: This could mean: (1) that the alcoves on both sides of the hallway all measured **six cubits**. It is implied that they were both six cubits wide and deep, Alternate translation: [six cubits each on both sides] or (2) that each alcove was **six cubits** wide and **six cubits** deep. Alternate translation: [six cubits wide and six cubits deep]

Ezekiel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the border on the other side was also one cubit]

13.note: The pronoun **its** refers to the alcove on the opposite side of the gateway. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from the roof of the alcove on one side to the roof of the alcove on the opposite side]

By **an opening in front of an opening**, Ezekiel means the measurement extended through the openings of the alcoves facing each other. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [through the opening of one alcove all the way through the opening of the other alcove that faced it]

14.note: This could mean: (1) that the **jambs** were **60 cubits** tall, Alternate translation: [60 cubits in height] or (2) that the **jambs** were **60 cubits** long in total. Alternate translation: [60 cubits long]

14.q: וְ⁠אֶל אֵיל֙ הֶֽ⁠חָצֵ֔ר הַ⁠שַּׁ֖עַר סָבִ֥יב סָבִֽיב
14.note: This part of the verse is difficult to understand. It could mean that the courtyard surrounded the inner part of the gate. It could mean that the man measured the jambs all the way around the gate, ending at the opening to the courtyard on the inside. That is the interpretation that the UST follows. You may want to follow the major translation in your area.
See how you translated “around, around” in verse 5. Alternate translation: [all the way around]

15.q: פְּנֵי֙ הַ⁠שַּׁ֣עַר ה⁠יאתון עַל־לִ⁠פְנֵ֕י אֻלָ֥ם הַ⁠שַּׁ֖עַר הַ⁠פְּנִימִ֑י חֲמִשִּׁ֖ים אַמָּֽה
15.note: The implication is that this measurement of **50 cubits** was the full length of the gateway, from its outer entrance to the far end of its porch on the inner side. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the full length of the gateway, from the front of its outer entrance to the far end of the porch of the inner gate measured 50 cubits]

16.note: The phrase translated as **shut windows** could refer to: (1) structures that were niches that looked like windows, but which did not go all the way through the wall. These nooks or niches could be used for storing things. Alternate translation: [And carved out nooks … And these nooks] (2) narrow or small. They may perhaps have been small on the inside and wide on the outside. Alternate translation: [And narrow windows … And these windows] or [And windows that narrowed as they went inwards … And these windows] (3) windows with coverings like shutters or lattices over them. Alternate translation: [And shuttered windows … And these shuttered windows]
See how you translated “around, around” in verse 5. Alternate translation: [all the way around … were all the way around]

Ezekiel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and thus there were shut windows for the porches]

17.note: The pronoun **he** refers to the man who was measuring the temple area, not to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the man who was measuring brought me to the outer courtyard]

The **chambers** were a series of side rooms, and the **pavement** was a path around the inside of the walls that were covered with flat stones. If your readers would not be familiar with what these things are, you could use the names of similar things that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [small rooms and a walkway paved with flat stones]
See how you translated “around, around” in verse 5. Alternate translation: [around the edges of the courtyard]

By **toward the pavement**, Ezekiel means that they opened onto the paved part of the courtyard. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [opened onto the paved walkway in the courtyard]

18.note: Ezekiel is using **to the shoulder of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to the side of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [was along the sides of the gates]

The implication is that this was called **the lower pavement** because it was lower than the inner courtyard. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the lower pavement, which was lower than the inner courtyard]

19.note: Ezekiel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. These words could be: (1) about which gate is being measured. In this case, Ezekiel is saying that they finished with the east gate and are going to the north gate. Alternate translation: [which completes the east gate; next was the north gate] (2) about what measurements the man took. In this case, the man measures both to the east and to the north. Alternate translation: [measuring to the east and to the north]

20.note: See how you translated the similar phrase, “gate whose face was the way of the east,” in 40:6. Alternate translation: [And the gate that faced north]

21.note: The phrase **its alcove** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. There is, however, a correction to make it plural in the margin of the text that Hebrew scribes have recommended. You may want to follow this correction in your translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Here and throughout the chapter, the UST follows the correction in the margin and makes it plural. See the chapter introduction for more information. Alternate translation: [And its alcoves]
See how you translated the same phrases “three from here and three from there” in verse 10. Alternate translation: [three on each side]

The implication is that **the first gate** is the gate on the east side that Ezekiel described in verses 6–16. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [according to the measurement of the first gate, the one on the east side]

22.note: The phrase **and its window** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. There is, however, a correction to make it plural in the margin of the text that Hebrew scribes have recommended. You may want to follow this correction in your translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Here and throughout the chapter, the UST follows the correction in the margin and makes it plural. See the chapter introduction for more information. Alternate translation: [and its windows]

The phrase **and its palm tree** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. There is, however, a correction to make it plural in the margin of the text that Hebrew scribes have recommended. You may want to follow this correction in your translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Here and throughout the chapter, the UST follows the correction in the margin and makes it plural. See the chapter introduction for more information. Alternate translation: [and its palm trees]
See how you translated the same phrase, “gate whose face was the way of the east,” in 40:6. Alternate translation: [the eastward facing gate]

The pronoun **they** and **their** refer to people in general, that is, anyone who would go up into the gateway. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And by seven steps people would go up on it and its porch was in front of those people climbing the steps]

The word translated as **to their face** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense, since the porch was on the inside end of the gate, not near the steps outside. The ancient Greek translation says “to the inside.” The UST follows that reading. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [was to the inside]

24.note: The implication is that using **according to these measurements** means that the measurements of the gates that Ezekiel has already described are the same as these. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [according to the same measurements as the other gates]

25.note: The implication is that using **according to these windows** means that the windows or niches that Ezekiel has already described are the same as these. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [these windows were the same as the other windows]
See how you translated “around, around” in verse 5. Alternate translation: [And windows went all the way around it and the porch]

The pronoun **it** refers to the gate or gatehouse, mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And windows were all around the gatehouse and its porch]

26.note: See how you translated the same phrase, “was to their face” in 40:22. Alternate translation: [was to the inside]

26.q: ל֗⁠וֹ אֶחָ֥ד מִ⁠פּ֛וֹ וְ⁠אֶחָ֥ד מִ⁠פּ֖וֹ אֶל־איל⁠ו
26.note: See how you translated the similar phrases, “three from here and three from there” in verse 10. Alternate translation: [were on each of the jambs]

27.note: See how you translated this similar phrase, “the way of the east” in verse 10 here and at the end of this verse.

Ezekiel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He means that the man measured **from a gate to the gate** on the inner wall to the corresponding gate on the outer wall. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the distance from this gate to the gate on the outer gate]

28.note: See how you translated this same phrases, “according to these measurements,” in verse 24. Alternate translation: [according to the same measurements as the other gates]

29.note: The pronoun **its** refers to the gatehouse on the south side. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the alcoves, jambs, and porches of the south gatehouse]

See how you translated “around, around” in verse 5. Alternate translation: [and its windows that went all the way around it and the porch]

30.q: וְ⁠אֵֽלַמּ֖וֹת סָבִ֣יב סָבִ֑יב אֹ֗רֶךְ חָמֵ֤שׁ וְ⁠עֶשְׂרִים֙ אַמָּ֔ה וְ⁠רֹ֖חַב חָמֵ֥שׁ אַמּֽוֹת

This reading, however, does not seem to make sense because it seems to contradict the measurements in the previous verse. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation, which does not include this verse at all. Alternatively, you may want to follow the major translation in your area.

This could mean: (1) that the porch for each of the three gates to the inner courtyard had these measurements, Alternate translation: [And there were porches for the inner gates] or (2) that the inner courtyard had porches with these measurements all around its outside boundary. Alternate translation: [And porches were all around inside the wall of the inner courtyard]

32.note: See how you translated these same phrase, “the way of the east” in verse 10.

33.note: The pronoun **its** refers to the gatehouse on the east side. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the alcove, jamb, and porch of the east gatehouse]
See how you translated the same phrase, “according to these measurements,” in verse 24. Alternate translation: [and they all had the same measurements as the ones in the other gates]
See how you translated these same words, “around, around” in verse 5. Alternate translation: [and the gate had windows all around including its porch and it measured]

34.note: See how you translated these same phrases, “from here and from there,” in verse 10. Alternate translation: [on each side of the opening]

35.note: See how you translated this same phrase, “according to these measurements,” in verse 24. Alternate translation: [and it had the same measurements as the other gates]

36.q: תא⁠ו אל⁠ו ו⁠אלמ⁠ו וְ⁠חַלּוֹנ֥וֹת ל֖⁠וֹ סָבִ֣יב סָבִ֑יב
36.note: The pronoun **its** refers to the gatehouse at the north side of the inner wall as mentioned in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [And the north gatehouse’s alcove, jamb, porch, and windows all around]
See how you translated “around, around” in verse 5.

37.note: The phrase **And its jamb** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. The ancient Greek translation says “its porch.” The UST follows that reading. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [And its porch]
See how you translated these similar phrases, “from here and from there,” in verse 10. Alternate translation: [were on either side of the jambs]

38.note: This could mean: (1) that the **opening** to the **chamber** was in the wall of the gate’s entryway, Alternate translation: [And there was a chamber, and its opening was in the entryway wall by the jambs of] or (2) that the **opening** to the **chamber** was next to **jambs** around the opening into the gate. Alternate translation: [And there was a chamber, and its opening was next to the jambs around the opening of]

This could mean: (1) that this kind of chamber was next to each inner gate, Alternate translation: [each of the inner gates] or (2) that this chamber was next to the north gate only. Alternate translation: [the north gate]

The word translated as **jambs** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed that a scribe may have misspelled the original word, resulting in this word. With slightly different spelling, it would say “porch,” which seems to fit better the meaning of this passage. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [were in the porch of]

The pronoun **they** refers to the Levites who worked in the temple and processed the meat for the sacrifices. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [there the Levites rinse the meat for the burnt offering]

39.q: שְׁנַ֤יִם שֻׁלְחָנוֹת֙ מִ⁠פּ֔וֹ וּ⁠שְׁנַ֥יִם שֻׁלְחָנ֖וֹת מִ⁠פֹּ֑ה
39.note: See how you translated the similar phrases, “from here and from there,” in verse 10. Alternate translation: [were two tables on either side]

Here, **to** marks the goal or purpose of tables as being for **slaughter.** Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [for slaughtering the animals used for burnt offering]

40.note: Ezekiel is using **to the shoulder** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to the side.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And off to the side]

Ezekiel is using **from to the outside** as a common expression of the culture to mean “on the outside.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on the outside]

The phrase **the one going up** could mean: (1) the steps going up to the gate, Alternate translation: [the steps going up] or (2) anyone who would go up to the opening of the gate. Alternate translation: [for anyone going up]

41.q: אַרְבָּעָ֨ה שֻׁלְחָנ֜וֹת מִ⁠פֹּ֗ה וְ⁠אַרְבָּעָ֧ה שֻׁלְחָנ֛וֹת מִ⁠פֹּ֖ה לְ⁠כֶ֣תֶף הַ⁠שָּׁ֑עַר
41.note: This could mean: (1) that there were four tables on each side of the steps and hallway through the gate, Alternate translation: [Four tables on the right side and four tables on the left side of the gate] or (2) that there were four tables inside the gate’s porch and four tables outside the gate next to the steps. Alternate translation: [Four tables inside and four tables outside to the shoulder of the gate]

Ezekiel is using **to the shoulder of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to the side of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the side of]

Here, **to** marks the slaughtering of the sacrifices as the goal or purpose of the eight tables. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [for slaughtering the sacrifices]

42.note: Ezekiel could be referring to: (1) **four tables** that he has already mentioned. These could have been the tables outside the gate. More likely, they were the tables inside the gate. Alternate translation: [And the four tables inside the gate] (2) **four tables** that he has not already mentioned. They may have been inside or outside the gate. Alternate translation: [And four more tables]

Ezekiel is using the possessive form to describe **stones** that are characterized by being **hewn**, that is, cut into shape out of the stone. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [were cut into shape out of stone]

By **they made rest the vessels**, Ezekiel means that these tables were for the utensils the Levites used for preparing the sacrifices. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [On these tables the Levites placed the utensils]

43.note: The word translated as **hooks** could refer to: (1) small shelves attached to the walls. Alternate translation: [And the shelves] (2) pegs protruding from the walls. These pegs may have had two points at their ends. Alternate translation: [And the two-pronged pegs]

The expression **were established** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, you could say that builders did it. Alternate translation: [were what builders had fastened in the house all around]
See how you translated “around, around” in verse 5. Alternate translation: [all the way around the walls]

Here, **to** marks the goal or purpose of these tables as being a place to put the meat to be sacrificed or **the flesh of the offering** Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [and the tables were for the flesh of the offering]

44.q: לִֽשְׁכ֣וֹת שָׁרִ֗ים בֶּ⁠חָצֵ֤ר הַ⁠פְּנִימִי֙ אֲשֶׁ֗ר אֶל כֶּ֨תֶף֙ שַׁ֣עַר הַ⁠צָּפ֔וֹן וּ⁠פְנֵי⁠הֶ֖ם דֶּ֣רֶךְ הַ⁠דָּר֑וֹם
44.note: The phrase **chambers of singers** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense since the Levites who were “singers” were not usually allowed in this part of the temple. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation which has “two chambers”, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [were two chambers in the inner courtyard. One was to the shoulder of the gate of the north, and its face was the way of the south]

Ezekiel is using **to the shoulder** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to the side” both here and at the end of this verse. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in verse 40. Alternate translation: [were to the side]
The pronoun **their** refers to the **chambers**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the faces of the chambers were the way of the south]

The phrase **of the east** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, may not seem to make sense since that gate would not open to the north. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation which says “gate of the south,” or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [the gate of the south]

45.note: The pronoun **he** refers to the man who was guiding Ezekiel and measuring the temple area. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the man who was guiding me spoke to me]

The man is using the possessive form to describe **the keeping** that is characterized by being done for **the house**, that is, the work of guarding and caring for the temple. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the ones doing the work of guarding and caring for the temple]

46.note: The man is using the possessive form to describe **the keeping** that is characterized by being done for **the altar**, that is, the work of guarding and caring for the altar. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the ones doing the work of guarding and caring for the altar]

The man is speaking of the descendants of Zadok as if they were his **sons**. He means that they all belonged to the family line of Zadok. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are the descendants of Zadok]

46.q: הַ⁠קְּרֵבִ֧ים מִ⁠בְּנֵֽי לֵוִ֛י אֶל יְהוָ֖ה לְ⁠שָׁרְתֽ⁠וֹ
46.note: The implication is that **coming near** to **Yahweh** means being allowed to approach his altar in order to serve him as priests, and that only the descendants of Zadok, out of all the descendants of Levi, were allowed to do this. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the only ones from among the sons of Levi who are allowed to come near to the altar of Yahweh in order to minister to him as priests]

The man is speaking of the Levites as if they were Levi’s **sons**. He means that they all belonged to the family line of Levi from whom all priests had to come. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the Levites]

47.note: Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of something. It means that the altar was located directly in front of the **house** which here means the temple building. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [was directly before the house]

48.q: וְ⁠רֹ֣חַב הַ⁠שַּׁ֔עַר שָׁלֹ֤שׁ אַמּוֹת֙ מִ⁠פּ֔וֹ וְ⁠שָׁלֹ֥שׁ אַמּ֖וֹת מִ⁠פּֽוֹ
48.note: The phrase **And the width of the gate was three** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation which reads “And the width of the gate was 14 cubits, and the shoulders of the gate were three cubits from here and three cubits from there,” or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. The UST follows the Greek translation. Alternate translation: [And the width of the gate was 14 cubits, and the shoulders of the gate were three cubits from here and three cubits from there]

49.note: The phrase **11 cubits** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense with the measurements in the following chapter. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation which reads “12 cubit,” or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. The UST follows the Greek translation. Alternate translation: [12 cubits]

The phrase **and by the steps** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not include the number of steps, as most other places in this chapter that mention steps do. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation that gives the number of steps as “ten,” or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [and by the ten steps]

This could mean: (1) that the **pillars** were outside, in front of the **jambs**, Alternate translation: [And pillars were outside, in front of the jambs] or (2) that the **pillars** were between the **jambs**, in the gateway, Alternate translation: [And pillars were in the gateway, between the jambs] or (3) that the **pillars** were connected to or part of the **jambs**, either on the outside faces or the gateway faces. Alternate translation: [And pillars were connected to the jambs]
